bottom_score.title: Bottom Score
bottom_score.what: The number of bottom signals that are currently true for this stock. In Phase 1 there are 4 signals (T1, T2, T3, S1), each worth 1 point.
bottom_score.why: One signal alone is weak. When several independent signals agree (price far down, oversold, near a long-term average, market in panic) the stock is more likely to be near a bottom.
bottom_score.how: 0–1 Normal · 2–3 Watch · 4–5 Strong bottom signals, research it · 6 Extreme. 'n/a' means a signal had no data and is not counted.
bottom_score.limits: It says nothing about the business. A failing company also scores high. Phase 2 adds a Quality Score to catch value traps.

near_200w_ma.title: T1 · Near 200-week moving average
near_200w_ma.what: The average weekly close of the last 200 weeks (about 4 years). The signal fires when the price is at most 5% above it.
near_200w_ma.why: For strong long-term companies the 200-week average has often acted as a floor in big sell-offs.
near_200w_ma.how: Price below or just above the line = historically cheap vs its long-term trend. Far above = extended.
near_200w_ma.limits: Needs 4 years of history (otherwise n/a). In a long decline the average itself keeps falling.

weekly_rsi.title: T2 · Weekly RSI oversold
weekly_rsi.what: The Relative Strength Index (14 weeks, Wilder's smoothing) compares the size of up-weeks with down-weeks on a 0–100 scale. Fires below 30.
weekly_rsi.why: Weekly RSI under 30 is rare for quality stocks and usually means heavy, maybe emotional, selling.
weekly_rsi.limits: A stock can stay oversold for months. It measures speed of the fall, not value.

drawdown.title: T3 · Deep drawdown
drawdown.what: How far the price is below its highest close of the last 52 weeks. Fires at 30% or more below.
drawdown.why: Big long-term buying opportunities usually come after large drops.
drawdown.how: −10% is a normal correction, −20% a bear market for that stock, −30% or more a deep drawdown.
drawdown.limits: A big drop can be fully justified by bad news. Check why it fell.

market_fear.title: S1 · Market fear
market_fear.what: Fires when the VIX is 30 or higher, or CNN's Fear & Greed index is 25 or lower. This is the same for every stock.
market_fear.why: Market-wide panic drags good companies down with the rest. Those are often the best long-term entry points.
market_fear.how: VIX ≥ 30 or Fear & Greed ≤ 25 = fear. VIX under 20 = calm.
market_fear.limits: Fear can last weeks or months. The CNN index is an unofficial source and may be missing (then only the VIX is used).

vix.title: VIX
vix.what: The market's expected volatility of the S&P 500 over the next 30 days, from option prices.
vix.why: It is the most common 'fear gauge' for US stocks.
vix.how: Under 15 calm · 20–30 nervous · above 30 fear · above 40 panic.
vix.limits: It measures expected swings, not direction.

fear_greed.title: Fear & Greed index
fear_greed.what: CNN's 0–100 index built from 7 market indicators (momentum, breadth, put/call, junk bonds, VIX and more).
fear_greed.why: Extreme fear has often lined up with good long-term buying moments.
fear_greed.how: 0–25 extreme fear · 25–45 fear · 45–55 neutral · 55–75 greed · 75–100 extreme greed.
fear_greed.limits: Unofficial data source that may break. US market only.

pct_from_52w_high.title: % from 52-week high
pct_from_52w_high.what: How far today's close is below the highest close of the last year.
pct_from_52w_high.why: Quick view of how much the stock has already fallen.
pct_from_52w_high.how: 0% = at its high. −30% = 30% below its high.
pct_from_52w_high.limits: Based on closing prices, not intraday highs.

data_check.title: ⚠️ Data checks
data_check.what: Every night the prices are checked for errors: zero prices, moves over 40% without a split, prices that stopped updating, and gaps.
data_check.why: Free data sources sometimes contain errors. A bad price should never trigger a score or alert.
data_check.how: ⚠️ next to a score = something looked wrong. A suspicious price is left out until the next run confirms it.
data_check.limits: Checks catch obvious errors only. See the Health page for each data source's status.

range_52w.title: 52-week range
range_52w.what: The lowest and highest closing price of the last 52 weeks, with today's price marked in between.
range_52w.why: It shows at a glance whether the stock trades near its yearly low (often where bottoms form) or near its high.
range_52w.how: Marker on the left = near the yearly low. On the right = near the yearly high.
range_52w.limits: One year is short for long-term investing. Use the 4-year average (T1) for the bigger picture.

sp500.title: S&P 500
sp500.what: An index of the 500 largest US companies, the most-watched measure of the US stock market.
sp500.why: When the whole market falls, good companies fall with it. That context matters when judging one stock's drop.
sp500.how: The day change shows how the market moved at the last close.
sp500.limits: US only, and dominated by the largest tech companies.

nasdaq.title: Nasdaq Composite
nasdaq.what: An index of all stocks on the Nasdaq exchange, heavy in technology companies.
nasdaq.why: Shows the mood in growth and tech stocks, which often move more than the overall market.
nasdaq.how: The day change shows how it moved at the last close.
nasdaq.limits: Tech-heavy, so it can differ a lot from the broader market.

support_resistance.title: Support & resistance
support_resistance.what: Price levels where a stock turned around before. Support is an old bottom below today's price; resistance is an old ceiling above it. The app finds them automatically on yearly, monthly, weekly and daily charts.
support_resistance.why: Buyers often step in again near an old bottom, so long-term investors use support zones to plan staged buys.
support_resistance.how: Stronger = seen on longer timeframes (yearly, monthly) and touched more often. An old ceiling that price broke through often becomes support (and the other way round).
support_resistance.limits: Levels are history, not a promise. A support can break, especially after bad news. Daily levels matter far less than monthly or yearly ones.

valuation_pct.title: V1 · Cheap vs its own history
valuation_pct.what: Compares today's price/earnings ratio (P/E) with the stock's own P/E over the last 5–10 years. Loss-making companies use price/sales (P/S) instead.
valuation_pct.why: A great company bought at a historically low valuation leaves more room for error and more upside.
valuation_pct.how: Fires when today's P/E is lower than 80 % of its own history (bottom 20 %). The range bar shows where it sits between its lowest and highest value.
valuation_pct.limits: A low P/E can mean profits are about to fall. Free data for EU stocks covers only about 4 years. ETFs have no P/E of their own.

insider_buying.title: V2 · Insider buying
insider_buying.what: Directors and executives buying their own company's shares on the open market in the last 90 days, minus what they sold. Share grants and option exercises are ignored.
insider_buying.why: Insiders sell for many reasons, but they usually buy for one: they think the shares are cheap.
insider_buying.how: Fires when insiders bought more than they sold (in value). Several insiders buying at once is the strongest sign.
insider_buying.limits: Only available for US stocks on free data. Planned sales and small purchases can be noise.

quality_score.title: Quality Score
quality_score.what: A 0–100 score for how healthy the business is, from its annual reports: financial health (Piotroski), bankruptcy risk (Altman Z), debt, free cash flow, sales growth, margins, share dilution and return on capital (ROIC).
quality_score.why: A low price alone isn't enough. A stock can be cheap because the business is failing. Quality tells a bargain apart from a value trap.
quality_score.how: 70 or more is High, 40–70 Medium, below 40 Low. Debt and ROIC count 1,5× (your choice). Each part shows the numbers behind it.
quality_score.limits: Based on free data: usually 4–5 years of annual reports. It looks backwards; a business can change fast. Not meaningful for ETFs.

verdict.title: Verdict
verdict.what: Combines the Bottom Score with the Quality Score into one word.
verdict.why: Bottom signals say the price is low; quality says whether the business deserves a second look.
verdict.how: Bottom Score 4+ and Quality 70+: Quality on sale. Quality 40–70: Check fundamentals. Quality under 40: Possible value trap. Bottom Score under 4: Not at a bottom.
verdict.limits: A shortcut to decide what to research first, not a buy signal.

moat.title: Moat (ROIC)
moat.what: Whether the company earns high returns on the money invested in it, year after year. ROIC = operating profit after tax ÷ (debt + equity − cash).
moat.why: Companies that keep earning well above their cost of capital usually have something competitors can't copy: a moat.
moat.how: Wide: average ROIC 15 %+, above the cost of capital (8,5 %) almost every year, and steady. Narrow: some of that. None: little of it.
moat.limits: Only 4–5 years of free data. Companies with lots of net cash can show odd ROIC values. Banks and insurers use return on equity instead.

piotroski.title: Piotroski F-score
piotroski.what: Nine simple yes/no checks comparing the last two annual reports: profit, cash flow, earnings quality, debt, liquidity, new shares, gross margin and asset turnover.
piotroski.why: Cheap stocks with improving fundamentals tend to do better than cheap stocks with worsening ones.
piotroski.limits: Only looks at the last two years, and a single big one-off item can flip a check.

altman_z.title: Altman Z-score
altman_z.what: A formula that combines working capital, retained earnings, operating profit, market value and sales to estimate bankruptcy risk.
altman_z.why: Avoids buying a 'bottom' that turns out to be the start of a collapse.
altman_z.how: Above 3 is the safe zone, 1,8–3 grey, below 1,8 distress.
altman_z.limits: Designed for industrial companies; not meaningful for banks and insurers (shown as n/a).

debt_quality.title: Debt
debt_quality.what: Net debt divided by a year of EBITDA (operating profit before depreciation), and how many times operating profit covers the interest.
debt_quality.why: High debt is the most common reason a cheap company doesn't recover.
debt_quality.how: Net debt under 1× EBITDA is comfortable, above 3–4× is a warning. Interest covered 8× or more is safe, under 3× a warning.
debt_quality.limits: Leases and off-balance items may be missing in free data.

fcf_quality.title: Free cash flow
fcf_quality.what: Cash from operations minus investments in equipment: the money left for owners.
fcf_quality.why: Profits can be bent by accounting; cash is harder to fake.
fcf_quality.how: Good when positive in at least 3 of the last 4 years.
fcf_quality.limits: Fast-growing companies may invest heavily on purpose.

growth_quality.title: Sales growth
growth_quality.what: How fast revenue grew per year over the last 3 years.
growth_quality.why: Shrinking sales are a classic sign of a value trap.
growth_quality.how: +10 % per year or more scores fully, −5 % or worse scores zero.
growth_quality.limits: Acquisitions and currency moves can flatter or hide growth.

margins_quality.title: Profit margins
margins_quality.what: Operating margin (operating profit ÷ sales) this year compared with its own average of the years before.
margins_quality.why: Falling margins can mean pricing power is fading.
margins_quality.how: Good when at or above its own average; 5 points below scores zero. A loss can never score fully.
margins_quality.limits: Cyclical companies swing a lot through the cycle.

dilution.title: Share count (dilution)
dilution.what: How the number of shares changed per year over 3 years.
dilution.why: New shares shrink your slice of the company; buybacks grow it.
dilution.how: Flat or falling is good; more than +5 % per year scores zero.
dilution.limits: Some companies pay staff in shares, which shows up here.

top_score.title: Top Score
top_score.what: The mirror of the Bottom Score: signs that a stock is getting hot (far above its trend, overbought, expensive vs its history, insiders selling, market euphoria, near a major ceiling).
top_score.why: Helps with the other half of investing: not chasing, and trimming positions that grew too big.
top_score.how: 0–1 Normal · 2–3 Getting hot · 4+ Consider trimming. Shown on your stocks only when it's 2 or more.
top_score.limits: Never a sell signal. Strong stocks can stay 'hot' for years.

far_above_trend.title: U1 · Far above its 4-year average
far_above_trend.what: Price compared with its 200-week (≈ 4-year) moving average.
far_above_trend.why: Prices far above their long-term trend tend to fall back toward it eventually.
far_above_trend.how: Fires when the price is 1,8× its 200-week average or more.
far_above_trend.limits: Fast-growing companies can stay far above their average for a long time.

weekly_rsi_high.title: U2 · Weekly RSI overbought
weekly_rsi_high.what: The weekly Relative Strength Index (0–100) measures how strong recent gains were.
weekly_rsi_high.why: Very high readings show buyers may have run ahead of the business.
weekly_rsi_high.how: Fires above 70; above 80 is very overbought.
weekly_rsi_high.limits: In strong uptrends RSI can stay high for months.

expensive.title: U3 · Expensive vs its own history
expensive.what: Today's P/E (or P/S) compared with the stock's own range of the last 5–10 years.
expensive.why: Buying at the top of its own valuation range leaves little room for disappointment.
expensive.how: Fires when today's valuation is higher than 90 % of its own history.
expensive.limits: A business that genuinely improved deserves a higher valuation.

insider_selling.title: U4 · Insider selling
insider_selling.what: Net open-market selling by directors and managers over the last 90 days, as a share of the company's market value.
insider_selling.why: Insiders sell for many reasons, but heavy net selling can mean they think the price is rich.
insider_selling.how: Fires when net selling is at least 0,05 % of the company's value in 90 days. A percentage is used because large companies' insiders sell every quarter.
insider_selling.limits: US stocks only on free data. Planned (10b5-1) sales can't be separated.

euphoria.title: U5 · Market euphoria
euphoria.what: CNN's Fear & Greed index for the whole US market.
euphoria.why: When everyone is greedy, prices tend to be high and risk is underestimated.
euphoria.limits: Measures the whole market, not this stock. The per-stock hype meter comes later.

near_resistance.title: U6 · Near a major ceiling
near_resistance.what: Whether the price is just below a major previous ceiling seen on monthly or yearly charts.
near_resistance.why: Old ceilings often stop rallies, at least for a while.
near_resistance.how: Fires within 3 % below a monthly/yearly ceiling zone.
near_resistance.limits: Ceilings do break; a breakout can turn it into support.

earnings_reaction.title: Earnings reactions
earnings_reaction.what: For the last 8 quarterly reports: the earnings per share (EPS) the company reported vs what analysts expected, and how much the stock moved the next trading day and over 5 trading days.
earnings_reaction.why: Shows how jumpy the stock is around reports, so a big move after the next one doesn't surprise you, and whether the company tends to beat or miss.
earnings_reaction.how: 'Typically moves ±7 %' is the average size of the next-day move, up or down. Beating estimates often isn't enough: the outlook (guidance) moves the price too.
earnings_reaction.limits: Estimates and dates come from free Yahoo data. A report after the close is measured from the next day's close.

risk_budget.title: Risk budget
risk_budget.what: How your money is split: core (broad and bond ETFs), satellite (single stocks and sector ETFs), speculative and cash, compared with your own targets.
risk_budget.why: Most long-term return comes from the core. Keeping single stocks to a slice limits the damage when a pick goes wrong.
risk_budget.how: Balanced default: core at least 70 %, satellite at most 30 %, speculative at most 10 %, cash at least 5 %. The black mark on each bar is your limit.
risk_budget.limits: ETFs are put in a bucket by their type, not by what they hold (the look-through comes later).

stress_test.title: Risk check: moves together and stress test
stress_test.what: Moves together: how closely the daily returns of two holdings followed each other over the last year (correlation, −1 to +1). Stress test: what your current holdings would have done in three real crises.
stress_test.why: Owning many stocks doesn't spread risk if they all fall on the same days. The stress test turns 'risk' into euros you can picture.
stress_test.how: Above 0,8 means they move almost in step. The stress test uses each holding's real move in that period; without that history, the S&P 500 (stocks/ETFs) or a bond ETF stands in.
stress_test.limits: Correlations change, often rising in a crisis. History doesn't repeat exactly.

twr.title: Time-weighted return
twr.what: How your investments did, with the effect of when you put money in or took it out removed. Each day's return is chained to the next.
twr.why: It's the fair way to compare your picks with an index or ETF: a big deposit right before a rise doesn't flatter you.
twr.how: Above the MSCI World line means your choices did better than the broad market over that period.
twr.limits: It doesn't show how much money you made: that's the XIRR and the 'what if' amount. Short periods are noisy.

xirr.title: Money-weighted return (XIRR)
xirr.what: The yearly return of your actual money: every buy, sale and dividend on its date, plus what it's worth today.
xirr.why: It answers 'how did MY money do', including the timing of your buys and sales.
xirr.how: Compare it with the ETF's XIRR for the same money: higher is better.
xirr.limits: Over a few weeks it swings a lot. Taxes you'll owe later aren't included.

what_if.title: What if you'd bought the ETF?
what_if.what: The same euros on the same days, put into the MSCI World ETF (IWDA.AS) instead, and what that would be worth now.
what_if.why: The honest test of stock picking: is all the effort better than the simplest alternative?
what_if.how: 'Ahead' means your choices beat the ETF in euros.
what_if.limits: Ignores the ETF's own small costs and the taxes of switching. Cash isn't counted.

yield_on_cost.title: Yield on cost
yield_on_cost.what: Yearly dividend divided by what you paid for the shares (your average price).
yield_on_cost.why: Shows what your investment pays you on the money you put in; it grows when a company raises its dividend.
yield_on_cost.how: Higher than the current yield means the dividend grew (or the price rose) since you bought.
yield_on_cost.limits: Says nothing about whether the stock is a good buy today: compare with the current yield.

dividend_forecast.title: Dividend forecast
dividend_forecast.what: Each holding's payments of the last 12 months, repeated one year later, times the shares you own now, after estimated taxes.
dividend_forecast.why: Gives an idea of the income your portfolio produces and when it arrives.
dividend_forecast.how: Bars show the month the money is expected in your account.
dividend_forecast.limits: Companies can raise, cut or skip dividends. Taxes are estimates from config/costs.yaml.

realised_gain.title: Realised gain or loss
realised_gain.what: What you got for a sale minus what you paid for those shares, both including costs.
realised_gain.why: Only sold positions count as realised: this is what tax rules usually look at.
realised_gain.how: Sales are matched to your oldest purchases first (FIFO), unless config/costs.yaml says otherwise.
realised_gain.limits: Starting positions use your average price as cost. No tax amount is calculated: verify the rules.

dividend_withholding.title: Tax withheld on dividends
dividend_withholding.what: Tax taken off a dividend before it reaches you: first by the company's country, then the Belgian roerende voorheffing.
dividend_withholding.why: It's the difference between the gross dividend and what lands on your account.
dividend_withholding.how: Part of the foreign tax can sometimes be reclaimed; check your broker's documents.
dividend_withholding.limits: The app's rates are estimates; your broker's statement is the reference.

thesis_rules.title: Thesis rules
thesis_rules.what: Numbers that must stay true for your reason to own a stock to hold, like 'sales growth at least 10 %'.
thesis_rules.why: Writing them down before problems start stops you from explaining bad news away later.
thesis_rules.how: ✅ all rules hold · ⚠️ one broke · ❌ several broke. A broken rule means: re-read your thesis, not automatically sell.
thesis_rules.limits: Figures come from yearly reports (via Yahoo), so they change a few times a year and can be missing for some stocks.

decision_log.title: Decision log
decision_log.what: Every buy and sell with one line of why and how you felt (calm, following your plan, FOMO, fear).
decision_log.why: Over months it shows which kind of decision works for you. FOMO buys often do worse than planned ones.
decision_log.how: Compare the average result per feeling. Rate each decision's process at the 3 and 12-month review.
decision_log.limits: A few trades say little: luck dominates small samples.
